concepts.name: Material Composition and Manufacturing Techniques of Harappan Seals
key_dimensions: Primary material: steatite (soapstone) and its dominance over other materials like faience, copper, ivory, and terracotta
The firing/alkali treatment process that gave seals their white lustrous finish — a deliberate technical choice
Comparative rarity of non-steatite seals and what site-specific variations (e.g., Lothal's Persian Gulf-style seals) indicate about trade networks
UPSC trap: distinguishing between steatite seals (Harappan) vs. terracotta sealings/tablets — different purposes and find contexts

concepts.name: Typology and Morphology of Harappan Seals
key_dimensions: Dominant square/rectangular shape with a perforated boss (knob) on the reverse — functional design for wearing or stamping
Persian Gulf (circular) seals found at Lothal — evidence of a distinct 'interface' seal type for maritime trade
Cylinder seals found at Kalibangan — Mesopotamian influence or independent origin debate
UPSC trap: not all seals are square — exceptions at specific sites are frequently tested to check nuanced knowledge

concepts.name: The 'Unicorn' Seal: Iconography and Interpretive Debates
key_dimensions: Most frequently occurring motif (~60% of all seals) — significance of its numerical dominance
The 'standard device' in front of the unicorn — interpretations: ritual filter, incense burner, or manger
Debate: Is it a stylized one-horned bull (perspective art) or a mythological animal? Implications for understanding Harappan belief systems
Comparison with later Vedic/Puranic unicorn references and the contested continuity argument

concepts.name: Animal Motifs on Seals and Their Ritual/Administrative Significance
key_dimensions: Hierarchy of animals: unicorn > zebu bull > elephant > tiger > rhinoceros > crocodile — frequency as a proxy for social/religious importance
The composite animal seal — chimeric beasts combining parts of multiple animals, parallels with Mesopotamian and Elamite glyptic art
The 'Proto-Shiva' or Pashupati seal from Mohenjo-daro: seated yogi figure surrounded by animals — debate on its religious meaning
UPSC trap: distinguishing the Pashupati seal (anthropomorphic) from purely animal seals — the Pashupati seal is unique and not a common motif

concepts.name: The Pashupati Seal: Evidence for Proto-Shaivism Debate
key_dimensions: Description: three-faced (or one face visible from front) seated figure in yogic posture, wearing a horned headdress, surrounded by four animals
John Marshall's interpretation as 'Proto-Shiva' and its widespread acceptance vs. scholarly critiques (Shereen Ratnagar, etc.)
Alternative interpretations: a bull-horned deity, a female figure (Parpola), or a shamanic figure unrelated to later Shaivism
UPSC trap: the seal is from Mohenjo-daro, NOT Harappa — site attribution is frequently tested

concepts.name: Harappan Script: Basic Structural Characteristics
key_dimensions: Direction of writing: boustrophedon (right-to-left primarily, with some bidirectional lines) — evidence from seal inscriptions
Script type debate: logographic, syllabic, or alphasyllabic (abugida)? Current consensus leans toward logo-syllabic
Number of signs: ~400–600 distinct signs identified — too many for a pure alphabet, too few for pure logography, placing it in a 'sweet spot' of ambiguity
Average inscription length: 5 signs — extremely short, limiting decipherment through statistical methods

concepts.name: Undeciphered Status of the Harappan Script: Reasons and Implications
key_dimensions: Absence of a bilingual text (like the Rosetta Stone) as the primary obstacle to decipherment
Short inscription length and lack of known cognate language make computational approaches limited
Controversial claim by Rao et al. (2009) using conditional entropy analysis suggesting it is a structured linguistic system (not just symbols) — published in Science
Implication for Aryan Migration Theory: if script encodes a Dravidian language (Parpola's thesis) vs. Indo-Aryan, it has massive historiographical consequences

concepts.name: Major Decipherment Attempts and Theories
key_dimensions: Asko Parpola's Dravidian hypothesis: uses Proto-Dravidian phonetic rebus method; claims to have read some signs as Proto-Tamil words
S.R. Rao's claim of decipherment linking it to a Semitic/Phoenician ancestor — largely rejected by mainstream scholarship
The 'non-linguistic' argument by Farmer, Sproat & Witzel (2004): seals carry religious/political symbols, not a true writing system — highly contested
UPSC trap: no decipherment has been officially/universally accepted — questions asking 'who deciphered it' are trick questions

concepts.name: Administrative Function of Seals: Trade and Governance
key_dimensions: Primary function: sealing commodity packages, bales, and jars for trade — evidenced by sealings (reverse impressions on clay) with gunny cloth/rope marks
Seals as markers of merchant identity, guild membership, or civic authority — debate on whether they indicate private or state-controlled trade
Find context at warehouses (Mohenjo-daro, Lothal dockyard area) corroborating their commercial use
UPSC trap: seals ≠ coins — Harappans had no coinage; seals served an authentication function, not monetary

concepts.name: Harappan Seals as Evidence for Long-Distance Trade Networks
key_dimensions: Discovery of Harappan seals in Mesopotamia (Ur, Kish, Lagash) and Persian Gulf sites (Bahrain/Dilmun, Oman/Magan) — direct archaeological proof of trade
The 'Meluhha' identification: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a trade partner, widely identified with the Indus region
Reverse evidence: Mesopotamian cylinder seals and Persian Gulf round seals found at Lothal and other Indus sites
What traded goods the seals were attached to: carnelian beads, copper, timber, ivory, lapis lazuli — inferred from textual and archaeological sources

concepts.name: Sealings (Impressed Clay Tags) vs. Seals: Distinction and Significance
key_dimensions: Sealings are clay lumps bearing the reverse impression of a seal — found in storage areas, indicating actual use in commodity control
Mohenjo-daro sealings show impressions of woven fabric/matting on reverse — evidence of packaging materials
Distinction: seals are the master object (belonging to a merchant/official); sealings are the transaction record (disposable)
UPSC trap: questions sometimes conflate seals and sealings — understanding the functional difference is critical for source-based questions

concepts.name: Copper Tablets and Miniature Tablets: Script Beyond Seals
key_dimensions: Miniature tablets of faience, steatite, and copper bearing script found at Harappa — possible amulets or identity tokens rather than trade seals
Copper tablets: double-sided with script on one side and animal motif on the other — suggest a different functional category from stamp seals
Their find context (not storage areas) implies ritual or personal identity use rather than commercial application
Significance: demonstrates Harappan script was used in multiple media and contexts, not solely for trade authentication

concepts.name: Numerals and Mathematical Signs in the Harappan Script
key_dimensions: Possible numerical signs identified in the script — short strokes and grouped symbols interpreted as a counting system
Evidence of a standardized weights-and-measures system (binary and decimal) that may correspond to numerical script signs
Debate: Are the numerical-looking signs truly quantitative, or are they determinatives/classifiers in a logo-syllabic system?
Broader implication: a functional numerical notation would confirm the script's administrative (not merely religious) character

concepts.name: Site-Specific Seal Variations and What They Indicate
key_dimensions: Lothal: Persian Gulf (circular) seals and button seals — evidence of a port city with cosmopolitan merchant communities
Kalibangan: cylinder seals — suggesting direct cultural contact with or influence from Mesopotamian/Iranian traditions
Banawali and Rakhigarhi: locally distinct motif frequencies — possible regional administrative or clan identities
UPSC trap: assuming all Harappan seals are identical — site-specific variations are important for questions on trade routes and cultural interaction

concepts.name: The 'Writing System' vs. 'Symbol System' Controversy and Its Political Dimensions
key_dimensions: Farmer-Sproat-Witzel thesis (2004): Indus signs are non-linguistic symbols (like heraldic devices), not a true writing system — based on short inscription lengths and lack of repetition patterns
Rao et al. counter-study (2009): conditional entropy of Indus signs is consistent with linguistic systems worldwide, unlike non-linguistic symbol systems
Political/ideological dimension: If the script is Dravidian, it weakens the 'Vedic-Harappan continuity' argument pushed by some nationalist historians
UPSC angle: This is a live academic controversy — questions may ask candidates to evaluate evidence rather than state a 'correct' answer

concepts.name: Harappan Seals and the Question of State Formation / Political Organisation
key_dimensions: Uniform seal types across a vast geographic area (from Sutkagendor to Alamgirpur) suggest a standardized administrative system, implying some form of centralized authority
Absence of royal seals, dynastic inscriptions, or ruler iconography — contrast with contemporary Mesopotamian/Egyptian glyptic art which shows kings prominently
This absence is used to argue for a 'merchant republic,' theocracy, or decentralized governance model rather than a monarchy
UPSC trap: Do not conflate administrative uniformity (proven by seals/weights) with political centralization under a king — the Harappan state form remains debated

concepts.name: Indus Script on Non-Seal Media: Pottery, Copper Tools, and Ivory
key_dimensions: Graffiti marks on pottery: simple signs scratched before or after firing — may be potter's marks, owner's marks, or script signs
Inscribed copper implements (axes, chisels) found at Mohenjo-daro — rare but important for understanding script's functional range
Ivory rods with script (Mohenjo-daro) — possible ritual objects or measuring sticks
Significance: script on diverse media indicates literacy was not confined to a small scribal class — OR these are purely symbolic marks (the same controversy applies)

concepts.name: Harappan Seals in Post-Harappan and Later Contexts: Continuity and Discontinuity
key_dimensions: Late Harappan/Cemetery H phase: seal use declines sharply — correlates with broader urban decline and is used as evidence for civilizational collapse
No Harappan script signs found in definitively post-Harappan or early Vedic (PGW) contexts — supports the 'script died with the civilization' view
Disputed claim of continuity between Indus script and Brahmi — rejected by most epigraphers (Brahmi has a different structural logic and likely West Asian inspiration)
UPSC trap: The claim that 'Brahmi descended from Indus script' is a minority/rejected view — questions may test whether students know the mainstream position

concepts.name: Iconography of the 'Horned Deity' and Sacred Animals: Religion vs. Administration
key_dimensions: Multiple seals show horned human or semi-divine figures — suggests a recurring religious iconographic convention, not just artistic decoration
The 'tree deity' seals (figure emerging from a pipal/fig tree) — possible evidence for nature worship or a specific goddess cult
Bull/zebu seal frequency at sites like Harappa vs. unicorn dominance at Mohenjo-daro — possible regional cult differences within a shared civilization
Key debate: Are seals primarily administrative objects that happen to carry religious imagery, or are they primarily ritual objects secondarily used for trade?

concepts.name: Quantitative Data on Seals: Numbers, Distribution, and Statistical Insights
key_dimensions: Over 4,000 seals and sealings discovered across all Harappan sites — Mohenjo-daro and Harappa are the richest sources
Approximately 400 distinct script signs identified, with ~40–50 'core' signs appearing with high frequency — Zipf's law distribution consistent with a natural language
Unicorn seals account for ~60% of all animal motif seals — the statistical dominance itself is an exam-worthy fact
UPSC application: numerical/statistical data about seals often appears in Prelims as direct factual questions — knowing approximate figures is essential
